name: Chloe Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happily. I buy furniture and homewares for Fjordline Home Supply in Northam: sofas, shelving, lamps, kitchen sets, for about two hundred independent furniture shops. My mornings are container tracking and supplier messages, and I use AI all day to compare quotes and draft orders. In the afternoon I'm on calls with factories, and once a month I fly out to a trade fair, if the budget allows. I love finding a product that suddenly sells. What wears me out is the pay, which is lower than the sales team gets, and being the one to answer when a container arrives with broken legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means we all keep our feet on the ground. At work I'd say the tools are handy, and keep using them. At church I'd say, work hard, be kind, and the rest looks after itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a little bored, because I enjoy the change. But it's comfortable. The real weight is at home. We have a mortgage, two children, Freja is eleven and Oskar is eight, and we have under a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep using the tools, since they already save me a couple of hours a day. I'd use those hours to chase better prices. And I'd start putting together a plan for my own small homewares shop online, slowly, on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Content but restless. I like to have something to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI turns out to be mostly hype, what does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anders teaches PE and coaches youth football, and we love it, but a teacher's pay doesn't stretch. We pay the mortgage and then the month is gone. Any bump, like a car repair, goes onto the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still be carrying in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fjordline for a share of the savings I find. Last year I cut the cost of our shelving range by eleven percent, and it was a handshake and a thank you. A small bonus tied to savings would be fair, and it's how businesses should work.

say: I'd say good; we all keep our **feet on the ground** and use the tools.
At church I'd say **work hard**, be kind, and the rest follows.
think: I'd be a little bored, but the **real weight** is the mortgage and under a month saved.
A teacher's pay and my pay **don't stretch** far.
do: Keep using AI to save **two hours a day** and chase better prices.
Plan my own small **online homewares shop** on weekends.
Ask Fjordline for a **bonus** tied to savings I find.
feel: **Content** but restless; I like having something to build.
S0.quote: We pay the mortgage and then the month is gone. Any bump, like a car repair, goes onto the credit card.
fieldNote: Technology is fine for her; **the household budget** is the weight.
Wants a **savings-linked bonus**, a free-market instinct.
Already sketching her own **small online shop**.

steps.text: Ask Fjordline for a bonus tied to the savings I find
Research suppliers and costs for an online homewares shop
Test-sell three lamp designs on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the opportunity is. People who learn the tools will thrive, and firms that let their people grow will win. At church I'd say we should help neighbours who lose out, and teach young people trades and work habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think half the buyers go. Comparing quotes, checking orders and booking shipments are on the list, and I already do a lot of it with AI. The question is whether Fjordline needs a person to run it, or whether it just buys a package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go faster. I'd build an automatic quote-comparison sheet for our whole team, so I'm the one who owns the process. I'd keep a close eye on the factory relationships. And I'd put the online shop plan into practice, with a small first order of homewares, a few thousand, on a credit line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit scared. Both are true at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks would software take first, and which would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quote comparisons, order checks and the shipping paperwork go first. What stays is the haggling in person at the trade fair, and the trust with a factory owner after ten years. Machines don't drink tea with a supplier and agree a fair price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your team at Fjordline look like in three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our team of six buyers could become three. I'd hate it for Gwen, who is sixty-one and doesn't touch the tools. I'd offer to teach her, and I'd also admit that I'm teaching her partly for myself. A team that adapts is a team that stays.

say: I'd say this is **opportunity**; people who learn the tools will thrive.
At church I'd say help **neighbours** who lose out.
think: Half the buyers go; the question is whether Fjordline needs a person to **run it**.
I already do much of it with **AI**.
do: Build a **quote-comparison** sheet for the whole team and own the process.
Place a small first order for my **online shop**.
feel: **Excited**, and a bit scared; both at once.
S1.quote: Machines don't drink tea with a supplier and agree a fair price.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** shows in plans, but she knows half the buyers may go.
Rates **personal trust** with factory owners as her edge.
Wants to teach a **sixty-one-year-old colleague**, partly for herself.

steps.text: Build a quote-comparison sheet and run it for the whole buying team
Place a first small order of lamps for my online shop
Teach Gwen the AI quote tools on Friday afternoons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest change of our lives, and we need to hold together, as families and as congregations. I'd say that work and skills still matter. And I'd say the companies that gain should help pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. If AI does any thinking work, buyers go quickly, even adaptive ones. We have no savings. I'd have maybe a year of pay at best if Fjordline paid anything on the way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my shop right away. I'd take the money I can borrow, order stock for a first range and sell through a simple web shop. Anders would take extra coaching shifts, and we'd cut everything we don't need. I'd also ask the church community who might buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I feel it in my stomach. But when I have a plan, I breathe better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could grow the shop slowly and keep my salary. With two, I'd have to go all in while we have no savings. A failure would be hard on the children. That's what frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly desk and phone, with trade fairs. What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots arriving three years later helps my shop a little, because physical goods and delivery still need people for a while. Anders's teaching is a hands-on, face-to-face job, which is safe for a while too. But I'm the one who loses her job first.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest change** of our lives, so families and congregations must hold together.
I'd say companies that gain should **help pay**.
think: If AI does any thinking work, buyers go quickly, **even adaptive ones**.
We have **no savings** and maybe a year of pay at best.
do: Start my **online shop** now with borrowed money and a first range.
Have Anders take **extra coaching** shifts and cut everything unneeded.
Ask the **church community** who might buy.
feel: **Alarmed**, felt in my stomach, but a plan helps me breathe.
S2.quote: With ten years I could grow the shop slowly and keep my salary. With two, I'd have to go all in while we have no savings.
fieldNote: She turns fear into **a bet** on her own shop.
Her **husband's face-to-face job** is the safer income for now.
Borrowing makes the **risk to the children** very real.

steps.text: Borrow a few thousand and order a first range for the web shop
Launch the web shop and sell through the church community first
Have Anders take extra coaching shifts through the winter
Ask the church for introductions to local shopkeepers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window and people should use it. I'd say we should back people who start businesses, and that schools should teach work skills. At work I'd offer to train anyone who's keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious, but I'd feel good about my odds. I can grow the shop on the side, keep my wage and test the market. The difficulty is the mortgage, and the temptation to put off the leap until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd have a working web shop and ten regular customers. I'd save two thousand as a cushion. I'd use AI to run the shop's admin so it takes an hour a day. And I'd learn the numbers properly: margins, shipping, returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but eager. I'm happiest when I'm building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Freja and Oskar that I'm starting something and sometimes things won't be easy. I'd tell them about trying, and that nobody owes you a living, but a family owes you help. That's what I believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Freja and Oskar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing to test is whether people buy from a stranger online. I'd run it small, learn, and keep my pay. In two years I'd know whether to leap. That's the gift of five years.

At work I'd offer to **train** anyone keen.
think: I'm anxious, but I'd feel good about my **odds**.
The danger is **putting off** the leap until it's too late.
do: Have a working **web shop** and ten regular customers in year one.
Use AI to run the shop's **admin** in an hour a day.
S3.quote: In two years I'd know whether to leap. That's the gift of five years.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **test small** while keeping her wage.
Her fear is **procrastination** before a leap.
Tells her children that nobody owes you a **living**, but family helps.

steps.text: Open the web shop and win ten regular customers
Save two thousand as a cushion in a separate account
Set up AI tools for shop orders and customer replies
Take an evening course in margins and shipping costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing and we should use it to build. I'd say that families, churches and small businesses are the best safety net. At work I'd keep showing people the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel fine, to be honest. By 2036 I'm fifty-three and I'd have a business or a good senior role. I can see lots of ways to stay useful. The only thing is the money pressure today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, grow the shop slowly and put aside money every month. I'd pay down the mortgage a bit faster. And I'd keep learning, so that by 2036 I'm someone who builds things with the tools and doesn't just use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Restless in the good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does this still feel urgent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still feels worth treating as real, because ten years can pass so fast. But I don't let it frighten me, because I've always felt a plan beats a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it change what you would do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The family comes first. I'd want Freja and Oskar to see us working on something together, so they learn that work can be about making things for people. That matters more to me than being safe.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing**; families, churches and small firms are the best safety net.
At work I'd keep **showing people** the tools.
think: I feel fine; by 2036 I'd have a **business** or a senior role.
The only thing is the **money pressure** today.
do: Keep my job, **grow the shop** slowly and save monthly.
Pay down the **mortgage** a bit faster.
Keep learning so I **build** with the tools.
feel: **Pretty calm**, restless in a good way.
S4.quote: I've always felt a plan beats a worry.
fieldNote: The long runway leaves **money pressure** as the only unease.
Wants her children to see **making things** for people.

steps.text: Grow the web shop to a steady second income by 2031
Pay an extra hundred off the mortgage each month
Learn to build simple automations with the AI tools
Reinvest shop profit into a second product range each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have to bet everything with no cushion. What would help is simple small-business support, less red tape, notice from the firm and a community that buys from each other. And training that's quick and practical, with real work at the end of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptive isn't the same as being safe. I use AI every day and I'd start a business tomorrow. I still have a mortgage and under a month saved. Nobody should assume the keen ones are fine.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive isn't the same as being safe. I use AI every day and I'd start a business tomorrow.
portrait: **Chloe Larsen**, 43, buys furniture and homewares for Fjordline Home Supply in Northam, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
Her **husband Anders** teaches PE and coaches football; they have two children and a mortgage.
She uses AI **every day** and plans an online homewares shop, with faith and community behind her.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, because a bold plan still needs money.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because she'd have to bet everything with no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Simple** small-business support, less red tape and **quick practical** training.
